mekki-muskil:1-1.t: His saying, the Exalted, {أَتَى أَمر الله}: it means "the command of Allah will come". The past form is good in place of the future because of the certainty of the coming of the command; so, in that it must inevitably come, it became like what has already passed and happened, and reporting it with the past was good. This occurs most often in what Allah, exalted be His mention, informs us will happen: because of the soundness of its occurrence and the truthfulness of the one reporting it, it has become as though it were something that has already happened.

mekki-muskil:15-15.t: His saying {أَن تميد بكم}: أن is in the position of accusative as a mafʿūl li-ajlihi (object of purpose). It has also been said its implied form is "out of aversion to its shaking (كَرَاهَة أَن تميد)", and it has also been said its meaning is "lest it shake (لِئَلَّا تميد)".

mekki-muskil:2-2.t: His saying {أَن أنذروا}: أن is in the position of genitive as a badal (substitute) from الروح — and الروح here is the revelation — or in the position of accusative on the dropping of the preposition, i.e. "with [the message] that: warn (بِأَن أنذروا)".

mekki-muskil:30-30.t:
His saying {مَاذَا أنزل ربكُم}: مَا is in the position of nominative as mubtadaʾ (subject); it is an interrogative whose meaning is affirmation (taqrīr). ذا means الذي and is the khabar (predicate) of مَا, and أنزل ربكم is the ṣila (relative clause) of ذا; with أنزل there is an omitted hāʾ referring to ذا, its implied form being "what is it that your Lord sent down (مَا الَّذِي أنزلهُ ربكُم)". Since the question was nominative, the answer ran accordingly, so أساطير الأولين is nominative, also as [part of] a mubtadaʾ and khabar, its implied form being "they said: it is the tales of the ancients".
As for the second, مَا and ذا are a single noun in the position of accusative by أنزل, and مَا is again interrogative; since the question was accusative, the answer ran accordingly, so He said قَالُوا خيرا, i.e. "He sent down good".

mekki-muskil:32-32.t: His saying {طيبين}: a ḥāl (circumstantial) from the hāʾ and mīm in تتوفاهم.

mekki-muskil:40-40.t:
His saying {كن فَيكون}: Ibn ʿĀmir and al-Kisāʾī read فيكون in the accusative, by conjunction to أن نقول [Translator's note: the text has أن تقول]. Whoever puts it in the nominative cuts it off from what precedes, i.e. "then it is"; what follows the fāʾ is resumed. The accusative as the answer to كن is far-fetched, because its wording is the wording of a command while its meaning is a report about the power of Allah, since there is no one there commanded to do anything; so the meaning is "We only say to it: Be, and it is". Its like in having the form of a command while not being a command is His saying, the Exalted, أسمع بِهِ وَأبْصر: its wording is the wording of a command and its meaning is wonder (taʿajjub). Since the meaning of كن is a report, it is far-fetched that فيكون should be an answer to it and be made accusative on that basis.
It is also far-fetched from another aspect: the answer to a command is made jussive only because it carries the meaning of a condition. When you say قُم أكرمك ("stand, I will honour you"), you make the answer jussive because it means "if you stand, I will honour you"; likewise when you say قُم فأكرمك, you make it accusative only because it means "if you stand, then I will honour you". This always occurs only with two verbs differing in wording and differing in agents. If they agree in wording and the agent is one, it is not permissible, because it has no meaning: if you said قُم تقم, قم فتقوم, اخرج فتخرج ("stand and you will stand", "go out and you will go out"), it would have no meaning, just as if you said "if you go out you will go out" or "if you stand then you will stand", it would have no meaning, because the two verbs and the two agents agree. Likewise كن فيكون: since the wording of the two verbs agrees and the agent is one, it is not good for فيكون to be an answer to the first. The accusative as an answer is permissible only remotely, by likening كن to a genuine command and likening [the two] to two differing verbs.
Al-Akhfash permitted, in His saying, the Exalted, قل لعبادي الَّذين آمنُوا يقيموا, that يقيموا be an answer to قل, though it is not truly an answer to it, because Allah the Exalted's command to His Prophet, peace be upon him, to speak does not contain an explicit command to them to establish the prayer, until he says to them: "Establish the prayer". So the accusative of فيكون as the answer to كن is permissible only by way of likening, as we have mentioned, and it is far-fetched because of the corruption of the meaning; al-Zajjāj permitted it. On this basis Ibn ʿĀmir read the accusative in Sūrat al-Baqara, Āl ʿImrān and Ghāfir. As for this sūra and Yā Sīn, the accusative is good, by conjunction to نقول, because أن precedes it.

mekki-muskil:42-42.t: His saying {الَّذين صَبَرُوا}: الذين is in the position of nominative as a badal (substitute) from الذين هاجروا, or in the position of accusative as a badal from the hāʾ and mīm in لنبوئنهم, or on the implication of أعني ("I mean").

mekki-muskil:51-51.t: His saying {إِلَهَيْنِ اثْنَيْنِ}: اثنين is a tawkīd (emphasis), in the same position as واحد in His saying, the Exalted, إِنَّمَا الله اله وَاحِد.

mekki-muskil:52-52.t: His saying {الدّين واصبا}: [واصبا is] accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial).

mekki-muskil:57-57.t: His saying {وَلَهُم مَا يشتهون}: مَا is nominative as mubtadaʾ (subject) and لهم is the khabar (predicate). Al-Farrāʾ permitted مَا to be in the position of accusative on the implied form "and they assign to themselves what they desire (ويجعلون لَهُم مَا يشتهون)". This is not permissible according to the Basrans, just as جعلت لي طَعَاما ("I made food for me") is not permissible; only جعلت لنَفْسي طَعَاما ("I made food for myself") is permissible. Had the wording of the Quran been ولأنفسهم مَا يشتهون, what al-Farrāʾ said would be permissible according to the Basrans. This is a principle that needs justification and much elaboration.

mekki-muskil:58-58.t: His saying {ظلّ وَجهه مسودا}: وجهه is the noun of ظلّ and مسودا is the khabar (predicate). In speech it is permissible to imply the noun of ظلّ in it and put وجهه and مسودا in the nominative as mubtadaʾ (subject) and khabar, with the clause as the khabar of ظلّ.

mekki-muskil:62-62.t:
His saying {وتصف ألسنتهم الْكَذِب}: اللسان ("tongue") is masculine and feminine. Whoever makes it feminine says in its plural ألسُن, and whoever makes it masculine says in its plural ألسنة, and so the Quran came. الكذب is accusative by تصف, and أن لهم is a badal (substitute) from الكذب, the substitution of a thing for a thing that is identical to it. الكُذُب has been read with three ḍammas, as a naʿt (adjective) of الألسنة, being the plural of كاذب, in which case you make أن لهم accusative by تصف.
His saying {لَا جرم أَن لَهُم النَّار}: أن is in the position of nominative by جرم, meaning "that has become due to them". It has also been said it is in the position of accusative, meaning "their deeds have earned them that the Fire is theirs". The original meaning of جرم is "to earn"; from it is المجرمون, i.e. those who earn sins.

mekki-muskil:64-64.t: His saying {وَهدى وَرَحْمَة}: two objects of purpose (mafʿūl li-ajlihi).

mekki-muskil:66-66.t:
His saying {مِمَّا فِي بطونه}: the hāʾ refers to الأنعام ("cattle"), because it is masculine and feminine: one says هو الأنعام and هي الأنعام; so this word runs on the dialect of those who make it masculine, and the one in Sūrat al-Muʾminūn on the dialect of those who make it feminine. This is related from Yūnus ibn Ḥabīb al-Baṣrī.
A second answer: the hāʾ in بطونه refers to "some", because من in His saying مِمَّا فِي بطونه indicates partition, namely those of them that have milk; so its implied form is "from what is in the bellies of some, which have milk", for not all of them have milk. This is the view of Abū ʿUbayda.
A third answer: the hāʾ in بطونه refers to "what is mentioned", its implied form being "We give you to drink from what is in the bellies of what is mentioned".
A fourth answer: the hāʾ refers to النَّعَم, because الأنعام and النعم are the same in meaning.
A fifth answer: the hāʾ refers to the singular of الأنعام, whose singular is نَعَم; نعم is masculine, and نعم is the singular of الأنعام. The Arabs turn the pronoun to the singular even if the plural wording has preceded; the poet — al-Aʿshā — said:
... فَإِن تعهديني ولي لمة ... فَإِن الْحَوَادِث أودى بهَا ...
(If you knew me when I had flowing locks — well, events have done away with them.)
He said بها and returned the pronoun in أودى to الحدثان or to الحادث, and made it masculine because it has no masculine from its own wording.
A sixth answer: the hāʾ refers specifically to the males; this view is related from Ismāʿīl al-Qāḍī. That indicated that the milk belongs to the stud: the milk is drunk from the females, yet the milk belongs to the stud, so the pronoun returns to it; and from this he argued that the milk in suckling [kinship] belongs to the stud (laban al-faḥl).
The hāʾ in His saying {تَتَّخِذُونَ مِنْهُ} refers to the singular of الثمرات mentioned before, so it refers to الثمر, just as the hāʾ in بطونه referred to the singular of الأنعام, which is النعم. It has also been said it refers rather to an implied مَا, because the implied form is "and of the fruits of the date-palms and the grapes is that from which you take…", so the hāʾ is for مَا, and من indicated it; dropping مَا is permissible just as dropping من is permissible in His saying, the Exalted, وَمَا منا إِلَّا لَهُ مقَام مَعْلُوم, i.e. "except one who has a known station": من was dropped because من in His saying وما منا indicates it. It has also been said that the hāʾ in منه refers to "what is mentioned", as though He said: "you take intoxicant from what is mentioned".
The hāʾ in His saying {فِيهِ شِفَاء للنَّاس} refers to the drink, which is honey; it has also been said, rather, it refers to the Quran.

mekki-muskil:8-8.t: His saying {وزينة}: accusative on the implication of a verb, i.e. "and We made [them] an adornment". It has also been said it is a mafʿūl li-ajlihi (object of purpose), i.e. "and for adornment".

mekki-muskil:106-106.t:
His saying {من كفر بِاللَّه}: من is in the position of nominative as a badal (substitute) from الكاذبين.
His saying {إِلَّا من أكره}: من is accusative as an exception.
The hāʾ in His saying {إِنَّه لَيْسَ لَهُ سُلْطَان} refers to Satan, may Allah curse him; it has also been said it is for the matter and the account [i.e. a pronoun of the matter].
The hāʾ in His saying {هم بِهِ مشركون} refers to Allah, exalted be His mention; it has also been said, to Satan, in the sense of "they, because of him, associate partners with Allah".
His saying {وَلَكِن من شرح بالْكفْر صَدرا}: من is a mubtadaʾ (subject) and فعليهم is the khabar (predicate).

mekki-muskil:116-116.t: His saying {لما تصف أَلْسِنَتكُم الْكَذِب}: الكذب is accusative by تصف, and مَا with تصف is a maṣdar (verbal noun). Whoever puts الكذب in the nominative with ḍamma on the kāf and the dhāl (الكُذُبُ) makes it a naʿt (adjective) of الألسنة. Al-Ḥasan, Ṭalḥa and Maʿmar read الكَذِبِ in the genitive with fatḥa on the kāf, making it a naʿt of مَا or a badal (substitute) from it.

mekki-muskil:123-123.t: His saying {أَن اتبع مِلَّة إِبْرَاهِيم حَنِيفا}: حنيفا is a ḥāl (circumstantial) from the nominative implied pronoun in اتبع; it is not good for it to be a ḥāl from إبراهيم, because it is a muḍāf ilayhi. The meaning of حنيفا is "inclining away from all religions to the religion of Ibrāhīm"; the root meaning of al-ḥanaf is inclining, and from it comes الأحنف (one with a clubfoot).

mekki-muskil:127-127.t:
His saying {وَلَا تحزن عَلَيْهِم}: the hāʾ and mīm refer to the disbelievers, i.e. do not grieve over their holding back from faith; His saying يمكرون indicates that. It has also been said the pronoun is for the martyrs concerning whom وَإِن عَاقَبْتُمْ to the end of the sūra was revealed, i.e. do not grieve over the disbelievers' killing of them. الضَّيق with fatḥa is the maṣdar (verbal noun), and with kasra (الضِّيق) the noun. The Kufans related that الضَّيق with fatḥa is in the heart and the breast, and with kasra is in a garment, a house and the like.
بِسم الله الرَّحْمَن [Translator's note: the opening words of the basmala for the next sūra, as they stand at the end of this entry in the source.]

mekki-muskil:73-73.t: His saying {مَا لَا يملك لَهُم رزقا من السَّمَاوَات وَالْأَرْض شَيْئا}: شيئا is accusative as a badal (substitute) from رزق. According to the Kufans it is accusative by رزق [as its object]; according to the Basrans رزق is a noun, not a maṣdar (verbal noun), so it does not govern except in poetry.

mekki-muskil:91-91.t: His saying {بعد توكيدها}: this wāw in التوكيد is the original, and it may be replaced by a hamza, so you say تأكيد. It is not good to say that the wāw is a substitute for the hamza, just as that is not good in أحد, whose origin is وحد, so the hamza is a substitute for the wāw.

mekki-muskil:92-92.t:
His saying {أنكاثا}: accusative as a maṣdar (verbal noun); its governor is نقضت, because it means نكثت نكثا ("she undid an undoing"), and أنكاث is the plural of نِكْث. Al-Zajjāj said: أنكاثا is accusative because it is in the meaning of the maṣdar.
His saying {دخلا}: a mafʿūl li-ajlihi (object of purpose).
His saying {أَن تكون أمة}: أن is in the position of accusative on the dropping of the preposition, its implied form being "by being (بِأَن تكون)" or "because of being (لِأَن تكون)".
His saying {هِيَ أربى من أمة}: هي is a mubtadaʾ (subject) and أربى is in the position of nominative as the khabar (predicate) of هي, and the clause is the khabar of كان. The Kufans permitted هي to be a separating pronoun (faṣl) with no grammatical position, with أربى in the position of accusative as the khabar of كان. This is the analogy of the Basrans' view, because they permitted هي, هو, أنا, أنت and the like to be separators with no grammatical position with kāna and its sisters, inna and its sisters, and ẓanna and its sisters, when after them comes a definite noun or what is close to definite; and أربى من أمة is among what is close to definite, because of the adherence of من to afʿal (the elative) and the length of the noun, since من and what follows it are part of the completion of afʿal. The Basrans made a distinction in this verse and did not permit هي to be a separator only because the noun of كان is indefinite; had it been definite, it would be good and permissible.
The hāʾ in {يبلوكم الله بِهِ} refers to the covenant; it has also been said it refers to the abundance and the rivalry in abundance.
